comparisons.peer_summary: AMD faces potential intellectual property infringement claims from third parties that could result in substantial damages, injunctions stopping product sales, or costly licensing and redesign efforts, any of which could have a material adverse effect on the business.
comparisons.comparison: While both companies disclose risks related to intellectual property litigation and potential injunctions, the specific context differs significantly. Qualcomm discloses risks arising from its active role as a licensor of standard-essential patents (SEPs) facing adverse interpretations by manufacturers and proposals to limit remedies like injunctions. In contrast, AMD discloses risks from being a defendant in third-party infringement claims where the outcome could lead to injunctions stopping product sales. Qualcomm's risk is about the valuation and enforceability of its own licensing portfolio against industry pressure, whereas AMD's risk is about defending against accusations of infringing others' IP.

sentences.text: Some manufacturers and users of standard-compliant products advance interpretations of these commitments that are adverse to our licensing business, including interpretations that would limit the amount of royalties that we could collect on the licensing of our standard-essential patent portfolio.

Others have proposed that injunctions should not be an available remedy for infringement of standard-essential patents and have made proposals that could severely limit damage awards and other remedies by courts for patent infringement (e.g., by limiting the base upon which the royalty rate may be applied).

With respect to intellectual property litigation, from time to time, we have been notified of, or third parties may bring or have brought, actions against us and/or against our customers based on allegations that we are infringing the intellectual property rights of others, contributing to or inducing the infringement of the intellectual property rights of others, improperly claiming ownership of intellectual property or otherwise improperly using the intellectual property of others.

These parties may file lawsuits against us or our customers seeking damages (potentially up to and including treble damages) or an injunction against the sale of products that incorporate allegedly infringed intellectual property or against the operation of our business as presently conducted, which could result in our having to stop the sale of some of our products or to increase the costs of selling some of our products or which could damage our reputation.

comparisons.peer_summary: Litigation to assert IP rights against customers or suppliers could harm customer relationships, while third-party IP litigation, including as a result of licensing activities, could negatively impact business financial condition and results of operations if IP protection is inadequate.
comparisons.comparison: Both Qualcomm and Broadcom disclose risks where their intellectual property licensing activities expose them to litigation. Qualcomm highlights that third-party proposals and adverse interpretations of its SEP commitments may limit remedies and devalue its patents. Broadcom specifically notes that its IP licensing business can result in third parties pursuing IP litigation against it, which could limit royalty collections. The comparison highlights a shared sensitivity to litigation triggered by licensing, though Qualcomm focuses on regulatory/standard-setting body dynamics while Broadcom focuses on direct litigation resulting from licensing relationships.

sentences.text: In addition, in connection with our participation in SDOs, we, like other patent owners, generally have made contractual commitments to such organizations to license those of our patents that would necessarily be infringed by standard-compliant products as set forth in those commitments (referred to as standard-essential patents).

For example, some have put forth proposals which would require a maximum aggregate intellectual property royalty rate for the use of all standard-essential patents owned by all of the member companies to be applied to the selling price of any product implementing the relevant standard.
Conversely, third parties have and may in the future pursue IP litigation against us, including as a result of our IP licensing business.

Any inability to adequately protect our IP could limit the value of our technology, result in the loss of opportunities to sell or license our technology to others or limit our collection of royalty payments, any of which could negatively impact our business, financial condition and results of operations.

comparisons.peer_topic: Intellectual Property Protection and Enforcement Risks
comparisons.peer_summary: Intel faces risks in protecting and enforcing its IP rights due to litigation, varying enforceability, and geopolitical factors, including compulsory licensing. Additionally, licensing practices and industry standard participation may allow competitors to use patents or exhaust rights, impairing IP value.
comparisons.comparison: Both Qualcomm and Intel disclose specific risks regarding the compulsory licensing of intellectual property rights and the impact of industry standard participation on patent enforceability. Qualcomm notes that third parties propose limiting injunctions and damage awards, effectively seeking to restrict remedies for infringement. Intel explicitly states that governments may adopt regulations requiring compulsory licensing of IP rights and that its participation in industry standards organizations requires it to offer licenses to competitors, potentially exhausting patent rights. Both face regulatory and legal pressures that can diminish the exclusivity and remedy options available for their patented technologies.

sentences.text: Others have proposed that injunctions should not be an available remedy for infringement of standard-essential patents and have made proposals that could severely limit damage awards and other remedies by courts for patent infringement (e.g., by limiting the base upon which the royalty rate may be applied).

Further, some third parties have proposed significant changes to existing intellectual property policies for implementation by SDOs and other industry organizations with the goal of significantly devaluing standard-essential patents.

From time to time, governments adopt regulations and governments or courts render decisions requiring compulsory licensing of IP rights, or governments require products to meet standards that favor local companies.
Our participation in industry standards organizations or with other industry initiatives at times requires us to offer to license our patents to companies that adopt industry-standard specifications.
